content: Most surgical procedures require an incision in the skin to provide access to the surgical site. At the conclusion of the procedure, these surgical wounds are typically closed completely. There are various methods available for closing surgical incisions, including sutures (stitches), staples, tissue adhesives, or tapes. Sutures used for skin closure can be categorized as either continuous or interrupted. Continuous sutures are generally placed in a subcuticular manner and may be made of absorbable or non-absorbable materials. In contrast, interrupted sutures are typically non-absorbable and involve the full thickness of the skin, although some surgeons may use absorbable interrupted sutures. The objective of this review was to compare the advantages and disadvantages of continuous versus interrupted skin closure techniques in patients undergoing non-obstetric surgical procedures. To achieve this, a systematic search of multiple databases was conducted in August 2013, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, and EBSCO CINAHL. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that directly compared continuous and interrupted sutures for skin closure were included, regardless of differences in the suture materials used. Studies were included irrespective of their language, publication status, year of publication, or sample size. Two independent reviewers identified eligible trials and extracted data. Binary outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. Meta-analyses were performed using both fixed-effect and random-effects models, and intention-to-treat analyses were conducted whenever possible. The review included five RCTs involving a total of 827 participants, with outcome data available for 730 participants (384 in the continuous suture group and 346 in the interrupted suture group). The participants underwent abdominal or groin surgeries. The reported outcomes included superficial surgical site infections, superficial wound dehiscence (wound breakdown), and length of hospital stay. However, other important outcomes, such as quality of life, long-term patient outcomes, and healthcare resource utilization, were not reported in these trials. The included studies were assessed as having unclear or high risk of bias. Across four trials, 6.5% of participants (39 out of 602) developed superficial surgical site infections. There was no statistically significant difference between the continuous and interrupted suture groups in the proportion of participants who developed superficial surgical site infections (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.40 to 1.33). Superficial wound dehiscence occurred in 23 participants (3.7% of 625 participants across four trials). Notably, 22 of these 23 cases occurred in the interrupted suture group. The risk of superficial wound dehiscence was significantly lower in the continuous suture group compared to the interrupted suture group (RR 0.08; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.35). Most cases of wound dehiscence were reported in two recent trials where the continuous suture groups used absorbable subcuticular sutures, while the interrupted suture groups used non-absorbable transcutaneous sutures. In the interrupted suture groups, the non-absorbable sutures were removed seven to nine days postoperatively, whereas the absorbable sutures in the continuous suture groups were not removed, as they were designed to be absorbed by the body. The continuous suture technique, using absorbable sutures, provides prolonged wound support without requiring suture removal. This difference in suture material and technique may have contributed to the observed reduction in superficial wound dehiscence in the continuous suture group. There was no significant difference in the length of hospital stay between the two groups (MD -1.40 days; 95% CI -7.14 to 4.34). In conclusion, the use of continuous subcuticular sutures may reduce the risk of superficial wound dehiscence compared to interrupted sutures. However, this finding is uncertain due to the low quality of the evidence and the potential influence of differences in suture materials. Continuous sutures used absorbable materials that did not require removal, whereas interrupted sutures used non-absorbable materials that required removal, which may have affected the outcomes. Differences in skin closure techniques have the potential to impact patient outcomes and healthcare resource utilization. Further well-designed, low-bias trials are needed to determine the optimal suturing method for skin closure.
